text: Every control in this chapter applies to privileged accounts too, but they get extra layers on top, because a compromised database sysadmin or domain administrator can touch almost everything, including the logging that would have caught the intrusion.

Privileged accounts are specifically database and server administrators, domain and cloud administrators, service accounts running with elevated rights, and emergency break-glass accounts. Any of these held permanently with no extra scrutiny is the single highest-value target an attacker can find.

A privileged access management vault changes how admins get elevated access. Instead of knowing a sysadmin password and typing it in, the password lives in a vault the admin doesn't directly know. They check it out for a session, and the vault can rotate the password automatically afterward, so even the admin who used it doesn't know the current value. That closes shared passwords that never rotate and no record of who used the account on a given day.

Just-in-time elevation, applied to admin rights specifically: an administrator requests elevation, states a reason, gets approved, and receives sysadmin for a bounded window, an hour, a maintenance ticket's duration. When the window closes, the elevation is automatically removed. A break-glass account is a last-resort credential for when the normal PAM system itself is down, used rarely, every use triggering an automatic alert. Session recording logs what commands ran during a privileged session, so there's a precise record if something goes wrong.

The account spends most of its time at normal-user privilege, briefly elevated only when there's an actual task. That closes Chapter Three's access controls. Next up: Chapter Four, data masking, the first of several ways to protect the data itself.
